summary: Bug hunt under his standing brief (#690): four areas, real touch/mouse input, every finding a failing test; one skeptic per finding; a fixer per area

confirmed.title: Pausing a clip with sound leaves the preview on an earlier frame than the playhead
confirmed.see: He stops playback on a moment, but the picture shows a frame from 2 to 8 frames (67 to 267 ms) before where the playhead actually stopped. A split, keyframe or bookmark he makes there lands on the playhead's frame, not the one he stopped on. Pressing . then jumps 3 or 4 frames at once.
confirmed.test: HUNT-a pausing a clip with sound leaves the preview on an earlier frame than the playhead — fails with e.g.: stopped at frame 39 (1.300 s) the preview shows frame 30 of the clip, 9 frames (300 ms) earlier, the clip left at 1.050 s; stopped at frame 55 shows 52; stopped at frame 99 (with a phone-sized 90 ms of sound latency) the preview shows frame 95, 4 frames (133 ms) earlier. It failed in every run at 1280 and at 380.
confirmed.evidence: js/app.js:2429-2458 FM.pause: FM.time = FM.snapFrame(FM.time) and then m.el.pause() for every element. It never calls FM.seekVideosToTime(), so the picture stays wherever the element was. During play the element runs behind the clock by an offset that the sync controller learns and keeps on purpose: js/app.js:1905 FM._syncBiasStep, with SYNC_WARMUP at js/app.js:1848 (#148 measured about 87 ms on a real import). Measured 55 to 300 ms here.
confirmed.fix: At the end of FM.pause, when not returning from review play, seek every forward clip to the snapped playhead (FM.seekVideosToTime(), ideally using the frameSeekTarget fix from finding 3). The seeked listener already repaints. A sketch of exactly this made the test pass.

verdict.reason:
I re-ran the test and it failed at both widths. At 1280 the stops read 38→33, 55→54, 70→68 and 100→96. At 380 they read 39→30 (element at 1.048 s, playhead at 1.300 s), 55→54, 70→69 and 100→95. The first stop, a normal play with no injected latency, missed by 5 frames at 1280 and 9 frames at 380, so the fault does not depend on the fourth run's artificial 90 ms seek-back. Stops 2 and 3 vary between runs (1 to 2 frames).

The code confirms the cause. FM.pause (js/app.js ~2429) snaps FM.time to a frame, then calls m.el.pause() on every element. It never calls FM.seekVideosToTime(), so the picture keeps whatever frame the element had reached. That is behind the transport by design. The sync controller learns the element's lag as bias and deliberately does not correct it (SYNC_WARMUP, _syncBiasStep, _syncMayLearn; queues 148 and 690 put it at about 87 ms on a real import and a 158 ms median on his phone). No 'pause' listener re-seeks the element afterwards. The 'seeked' repaint only fires after a seek, and nothing issues one.

So on his phone a paused video shows a frame 2 to 5 or more frames before the playhead. Meanwhile shapes, text, the timecode, splits, keyframes and the export all use FM.time. The paused picture is not the frame he will cut or export at, and the next press of '.' seeks from FM.time, so the video jumps several frames at once.

The rest of the fixture holds up. The clip is an ordinary one with sound. Space is dispatched to the app's own keydown handler, and the handler runs the same code as a real key press. The canvas reader's controls pass. I found no request in REQUESTS.md or INBOX.md asking pause to keep the element's frame, and the pause snap goes back to v2.53 "frame-accurate timeline", which aimed for frame accuracy.

One caveat on the fix. Seeking to the playhead on pause means the picture moves forward a few frames the moment he pauses. The other option is to move the playhead back to the element's frame. That choice between the two is his, but either way the current mismatch is a real defect.

confirmed.title: Tapping the play pill to stop lets playback run a quarter second past the tap

confirmed.test: HUNT-a tapping the play pill to stop lets playback run on a quarter second past the tap — fails with: at 380 px he tapped at 1.704 s and playback stopped at 1.933 s, 229 ms (7 frames) later; at 1280 px he clicked at 1.629 s and playback stopped at 1.867 s, 237 ms (7 frames) later. It uses a real touch at 380 and a real mouse at 1280. The mouse half runs only when the driver window is wide enough.

The 240 ms wait exists so a double-click does not START playback, but it also delays the pause. The dblclick handler (js/app.js:6384) already pauses anyway, so the delay does nothing useful when stopping.

verdict.reason:

confirmed.title: Stepping or scrubbing a 30 fps clip never shows every third frame, and shows the frame before it twice
confirmed.see: When he steps frame by frame with . or , or drags the timeline to line up a cut, the preview reads 0,1,1,3,4,4,6,7,7 … Frames 2, 5, 8, 11 … never appear and the frame before each one shows twice. The frame he parks on and cuts at is not the frame the export shows there, because HUNT-d fixed the export but not the preview.
confirmed.test: HUNT-a stepping a 30 fps clip frame by frame skips every third frame and shows the one before it twice — fails with: pressing . from 0 the preview reads 0,1,1,3,4,4,6,7,7,9,10,10,12,13,13,15, so source frame(s) 2, 5, 8, 11, 14 never appear …; on the scrub path scrubbed to frame 26 it shows 25, 41 shows 40, 44 shows 43; stepping back with , frame 11 shows 10, frame 8 shows 7. This is deterministic at both widths.

verdict.reason:
I re-ran the test in the hunt5-a worktree at desktop width and again at 380px. It failed the same way both times, with the same numbers: pressing . from frame 0 the preview reads 0,1,1,3,4,4,6,7,7,9,10,10,12,13,13,15. Scrubbing to frame 26 shows 25, 41 shows 40 and 44 shows 43; stepping back with , frame 11 shows 10 and frame 8 shows 7. The control frames (0, 1, 3, 4 and so on) read correctly, so the frame reader and the clip are fine.

The code path matches the report:
- The . key (js/app.js:8161) calls FM.setTime, which snaps to the frame grid and calls FM.seekVideosToTime. The timeline scrub (FM.scrubTime) reaches the same function one animation frame later.
- FM.seekVideosToTime (js/app.js:1208-1220) writes the bare k/30 time into m.el.currentTime.
- For a forward clip the compositor draws m.el directly (js/compositor.js, the `src = m.el` branch). The frame cache is only used for reversed or frame-blend clips, so what he sees paused is whatever frame that seek lands on.
- FM.frameSeekTarget (js/frames.js:59) adds half a millisecond so the seek lands inside the frame. Its own comment records this exact 1,1,3,4,4,6 pattern on a bare element. The fixture is not an artefact. Frame timestamps sit exactly on the k/30 grid, the same layout a 30 fps phone recording has, and Chrome handles it the same way. - Clearing rec.stripFrames only keeps the timeline thumbnails from seeking the same video element during the test. It does not change which frame the preview seek lands on.

No REQUESTS.md entry makes this intended behaviour.

He hits this on his PC in Chrome or Edge, which is where he steps with . and , and scrubs to line up a cut. The frame he parks on is one before the frame that exports at a third of the stops.

Caveat: his phone is an iPhone 16 Pro Max (Safari/WebKit), which turns a seek time into a video position differently from Chrome. I could not check the phone half here. The effect there may differ or not appear, so "high" is about right for PC but unproven for the phone.

confirmed.title: Leaving the app mid-play: the playhead keeps running while he is away, and the clip keeps sounding past its cut
confirmed.see: He is previewing, switches to another app or tab for a couple of seconds and comes back. The playhead has jumped ahead by the whole time he was away, or run to the end and stopped, so he has lost his place. On the PC, a clip trimmed shorter than its source keeps playing its sound in the background tab well past its cut, because nothing stops it at its end.
confirmed.test: HUNT-a leaving the app mid-play and coming back finds the playhead seconds further on with the clip still sounding — fails with: he left at 1.00 s and came back 2.5 s later to the playhead at 3.75 s, still playing; while he was away the clip kept sounding (its element at 3.40 s, past its cut at 1.50 s) with nothing to stop it at its end. The test fakes the background the way a browser does it: document.hidden, visibilitychange and requestAnimationFrame held while hidden.
confirmed.evidence: There is no playback handler for visibilitychange or pagehide anywhere in js/app.js. The only listeners are in js/audio-health.js:273-274, and they just save a report; their comment assumes playback is torn down when he leaves. tick (js/app.js:2236) stops being called while the page is hidden, but FM.playing stays true and FM.clockNow (js/app.js:1709) keeps counting wall time. So the first tick back jumps the playhead, and the clip's <video> element keeps playing on its own with no tick to pause it at the end of its clip window.
confirmed.fix: Pause playback on a hidden visibilitychange and on pagehide: document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => { if (document.hidden && FM.playing) FM.pause(); }). The sketch passed the test.

verdict.reason:
I re-ran the test against the hunt5-a worktree, using the server already running on 8961 from that folder. It fails the same way the hunter reported: he left at 1.00 s, came back 2.5 s later, and the playhead was at 3.77 s and still playing. The clip's element was at 3.35 s, past its cut at 1.50 s. The control passed, so playback really was running with the clip sounding before he left.

The code path shows the same thing.
- The only playback loop is tick (js/app.js:2236), and it runs only on requestAnimationFrame, which a real hidden page stops calling.
- FM.clockNow (js/app.js:1709) works out the playhead from performance.now() since play started, so the first tick back jumps by however long he was away. If that passes the end, tick pauses at P.duration and his place is lost.
- The rule that stops a clip at its cut (pause and mute when the playhead leaves the clip) lives only in syncMediaToClock, which only tick calls. Nothing on a timer, timeupdate or frame callback enforces it, so while the page is hidden the element plays on its own.
- Nothing in js/app.js pauses playback on visibilitychange or pagehide. The only such listener, js/audio-health.js:273-274, just saves a report, and its own comment assumes playback is stopped when he leaves.

The simulation is fair. The browser really does report document.hidden and fire visibilitychange, and a real hidden page really does stop requestAnimationFrame. Timers were not slowed in the test, but that changes nothing because no timer drives playback.

REQUESTS.md has no request asking for playback to carry on in the background. Voice recording already stops when the app is hidden (js/voice-rec.js bgStop), so stopping on hide is how the rest of the app behaves.

What he would actually hit depends on the device:
- On the PC, after switching tabs or minimising the window, the cut clip's sound runs on past its cut until the source ends. Other clips that should start never sound. Coming back, the playhead has jumped or stopped at the end.
- On his iPhone, iOS pauses the video element in the background, so the sound half probably does not happen. The playhead jump does: a plain clip uses the wall clock, and a stopped audio clock also hands the full time away to the playhead. So he comes back to a playhead seconds further on, or stopped at the end, and loses his place.

The visible half is real on both devices and the audible half is real on the PC. Medium severity is reasonable, perhaps leaning low on the phone.

This is a real bug, but his window to hit it is narrow for a normal song. It gets wide for long audio, big GIFs, and taking the audio out of a video.

**Re-run:** I ran it on port 8964 against the hunt5-d worktree with `?only=song still opening`. It fails as described in about 5.4s. The control passes: the same #file-input picker adds a song normally. So the red comes from the bug, not the rig.

**Code path (js/app.js handleFiles, around lines 5121–5147):** it awaits `FM.loadVideoFile` / `loadImageFile` / `audioFromVideo`, then calls `FM.addMediaLayer(rec)`. `addMediaLayer` (app.js:2788) reads `FM.scene` at call time. It inserts the layer, commits history, saves, and records the clip in the media library, all in whatever project is open by then. Nothing records which project the pick was made in. Nothing on the plain song/video/GIF path stops him leaving meanwhile: no overlay or busy flag, and #m-back goes straight to `FM.home.open()`. The loading dot only appears after the layer has landed.

**It matches rules the app already follows:**
- medialib.js `use()` captures `openProjectId()` before its first await and gives up with 'Not added — you switched projects' (915.5B).
- ai-chat.js does the same for AI replies (queue 690, hunt f).
- REQUESTS.md records the AI Director version of this exact bug as [medium], fixed in v16.94.

He has not asked for this behaviour anywhere. A song landing in a project he never added it to, and missing from the one he picked it in, is plainly wrong.

**How reachable it is:**
- The hold in the test is artificial, but it only stands in for a real, unguarded await.
- I measured the real window on this Mac: a 4-minute 192 kbps AAC song reads its metadata in 3–19 ms, then `decodeAudioData` takes about 310–360 ms. On a phone that is probably under a second or so. Going back, waiting for Home and tapping another card takes a person roughly 1.5 s or more, so with a typical song he would rarely manage it.
- The window grows with the file, and the decode is allowed up to 300 MB (WAVE_MAX_BYTES). A 20–30 minute mix or podcast, or a many-frame GIF, gives him several seconds.
- The Add ▸ Audio route that takes the sound out of a video is wider still. It decodes at the device rate, builds a WAV, and shows 'Taking the audio out of…' while he waits. Nothing stops him leaving, and the result lands in the wrong project the same way.

After each await, check it again; if the project has changed, abandon the rest of the batch and toast using 915.5B's wording.
